paragraphs: Katub battora: "lo tebashshel gedi bachaleb immo" shalosh peamim (shemot kg, yt; sham ld, kv; debarim yd, k). veqibbelu chaza"l: echad leissur akila, veechad leissur bishshul, veechad leissur hanaa. veod qibbelu: "g diktib "gedi" - lav davqa, ella hu haddin kol basar behema tehora asur, ella sheddibber hakkatub bahoveh, deken haya hadderek lebashshel gedayim bechalab. veod qibbelu: la shena bachaleb em, la shena bechalab acheret. veod qibbelo, shehotzi hakkatub issur akila bilshon bishshul, lilmod deeno asur min hattora baakila, ella-im-ken hu naaseh derek bishshul, abal im nibla zeh bazeh "y kebisha, shennikbash habbasar bechalab k"d shaot, o "y melicha shennimlechu beyachad, hare zeh muttar baakila min hattora, veraq middibre soperim asur baakila bekol inyan - hen "y kibbush, hen "y melicha - velaken muttar leyisrael likbosh legoy basar bechalab, o limloach lo basar im hechalab; veayyen "peri-toar", siman tz", seip qatan y"z; veraq bishshul asur leyisrael, lebashshel legoy basar bechalab, deober belav apillu shehu mebashshel laggoy.

clarification.explanation: The Torah writes three times "you shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk" — and from this our Sages derived three separate laws: the prohibition of eating meat and milk together, the prohibition of cooking them together, and the prohibition of deriving any benefit from them. Although the Torah wrote "kid," this is not exclusive — the law is the same for the meat of any pure domestic animal, but the Torah spoke of the common case of that time. Likewise, the law is the same whether it is the milk of the kid's own mother or the milk of another animal. Furthermore: the Torah phrased the eating prohibition in terms of "cooking" — from which we learn that the Torah-level eating prohibition applies only when the meat and milk were mixed through actual cooking. But if they were absorbed into each other another way — for example, through pickling (soaking the meat in milk for 24 hours) or joint salting — this is forbidden for eating only rabbinically, not by Torah law. Therefore a Jew is permitted to pickle or salt meat and milk together on behalf of a gentile, but a Jew is forbidden to cook meat in milk for a gentile, since cooking itself is a Torah-level prohibition even when cooking for a gentile's sake.
takeaways: The prohibition of meat and milk comprises three separate Torah-level prohibitions: eating, cooking, and benefit.
The Torah-level prohibition applies only when the mixture was made by cooking; pickling or joint salting are only rabbinically forbidden, so a Jew may do this for a gentile (but not cook for him).

paragraphs: Shiur bishshul, la baenan sheyyitbashshel kemaakal ben derosay, ella kol shennapal chatikat basar bikli rishon shel chalab shehu al haesh, apillu shehesirah miyyad, hare zeh asur baakila ubahanaa. veayyen "kareti", seip qatan g, v"peri-megadim" bappeticha, ot g'. v"g deen chiyyub milleqiyyot ella beshiur kazzayit, mikkol maqom chatzi shiur asur min hattora gam bebishshul ubahanaa. veayyen "erek-hashshulchan" v"pitche-teshuba" beshem haggaon tzl"ch za"l. velaken gam im bishshel pachot mikkazzayit, abar issur tora vetzarik kappara.

clarification.explanation: Regarding the prohibition of cooking meat in milk, the dish need not be fully cooked (to the point of "Ben Drosai" food) — it suffices for a piece of meat to fall into a first vessel (a vessel standing directly on the fire) containing boiling milk, even if removed immediately — and this is already forbidden for eating and for benefit. Although the penalty of lashes is given only for eating a measure of an olive's volume, nevertheless even less than that measure is Torah-forbidden — both for cooking and for benefit — and one who transgressed this needs atonement, even though not lashed.
takeaways: A piece of meat falling into a first vessel with boiling milk forbids it immediately, even if removed right away.
Even less than an olive's volume is Torah-forbidden for cooking and benefit, though it carries no lash penalty; atonement is still needed.

paragraphs: Basar bechalab haasur bahanaa, tzarik lo qebura; velaken nohagim lishpok oto bachapira sheyyesh bechatzer sheqqorin bearbe "beloa" (bor shopekin), vezo hi qeburato, o yashlikennu lannahar haggadol beopen sheyyitabbed; veayyen keneset haggedola vechakemat adam; abal asur litteno legoy, apillu sheeno makkiro; veken asur litteno lekeleb, apillu keleb dealema sheen lo hanaa mimmennu. velaken asur lezareqo birshut- harabbim, ki sham okelim oto hakkelabim; vekol shekken lekalbo deasur, shehare neheneh mimmennu.

clarification.explanation: Meat and milk forbidden for benefit must be "buried" — that is, poured into a sewage pit in the courtyard, or thrown into a large river so it disappears entirely. It is forbidden to give it to a gentile, even a stranger unknown to him, and it is forbidden to give it even to a dog — even an ownerless dog from which a Jew derives no benefit, since any benefit whatsoever from the mixture is forbidden. For this reason it is also forbidden to throw it in a public domain, since dogs would eat it there, which is an indirect benefit, and all the more so it is forbidden to feed it to one's own dog, where the benefit is clear.
takeaways: Meat and milk forbidden for benefit require "burial" (disposal in a sewage pit or river), and may not be given to a gentile or a dog in any form, including throwing it in a public domain.

paragraphs: Basar bechalab hanneesar "y kibbush o melicha - kevan deeno asur min hattora baakila, ella raq middibre soperim - hare zeh muttar bahanaa, umikkol maqom asur lebashshelo; veim chazar ubishshelo, hare zeh asur bahanaa min hattora, vegam chayyab mishshum bishshul; veayyen "peri-megadim" biptichato. veken hu haddin debar maakol shel hetter, kegon orez o yeraqot vekayyotze, shennibla bahem basar vegam nibla bahem chalab, uben shenehem yesh shiur kazzayit, veaach"k bishshel hammaakol hahu - hare zeh ober alayv; abal im nibla baqqedera basar vegam chalab, "p sheyyesh ben shenehem kazzayit, veshub bishshel baqqedera hahi tabshil - "p sheen bo shishshim neged habbalua, eno ober mishshum issur bishshul, mippene sheen echad mehem beayin, ella hakkol hu balua. mihu qedera shebbalea chalab, ubeodah bat-yomah bishshel bah basar beayin, ober alayv mishshum bishshul, mippene deechad mehem hu beayin; veayyen sipte daat, seip qatan y"ch, umachaziq beraka, ot k"b; velaken zeh hambashshel biqdera zo, bae kappara kishar issure lavyan.

clarification.explanation: Meat and milk forbidden through pickling or salting (not cooking) — since the prohibition is only rabbinic, not Torah-level — may be benefited from, but it is still forbidden to cook them. And if they were nevertheless cooked after the pickling or salting, this now becomes forbidden for benefit as well, by actual Torah law, and one becomes liable also for the cooking prohibition. The same rule applies to a permitted food (such as rice or vegetables) that absorbed both meat and milk (together totaling an olive's measure), and this food was then cooked — this is a prohibition. But if it was the pot itself (not the food) that absorbed meat and milk together, and a dish was then cooked in it, this is not considered a new cooking prohibition, since in the pot everything is "absorbed" rather than "actual" (not visibly present). But if actual meat (visibly present) was placed in a pot that had already absorbed milk that same day ("within its day"), this does forbid due to cooking, since here one of the two (the meat) is actually present.
takeaways: Meat and milk mixed through pickling/salting may be benefited from but not cooked; if cooked, they become forbidden for benefit too.

A pot that absorbed meat and milk together (both absorbed, not actual) cooking a dish is not a new cooking prohibition; but placing actual meat in a pot that absorbed milk that same day does forbid due to cooking.

paragraphs: Basar bechalab deasur min hattora bebishshul ubahanaa, lav davqa basar shel behema tehora keshera, ella apillu besar nebela uterepa shel behema tehora, asur min hattora bebishshul ubahanaa; veayyen sipte daat umachaziq beraka; abal besar behema temea bachaleb behema tehora, o besar behema tehora bachaleb behema temea, hare zeh muttar bebishshul ubahanaa, debaenan duvmya digdi bachaleb immo, shehu basar tahor bachaleb tehora. umikkol maqom asur lebashshel lekattechilla besar behema temea bachaleb tehora o lehepek, mippene marit haayin, sheharoeh chosheb shehu basar tahor bachaleb tehora; veod, choshedo debae leekol. veayyen machaziq beraka, ot ch', bedibbur hammatchil "hadran ledidan veku'", yeuyyan sham. umihu letzorek repua, apillu lecholeh sheen bo sakkana, muttar lebashshel. veayyen keneset haggedola, haggahat bet yosep, ot t', ushear acharonim za"l.

clarification.explanation: The Torah-level prohibition of meat and milk (in cooking and benefit) is not limited to the meat of a kosher pure domestic animal — even the meat of a nevelah or treifah pure domestic animal is Torah-forbidden when cooked with milk, for both cooking and benefit. But the meat of an impure animal (such as a pig) with the milk of a pure animal, or vice versa, is Torah-permitted for cooking and benefit, since the Torah-level prohibition applies specifically to a case resembling "a kid in its mother's milk" — that is, pure meat with pure milk. Nevertheless, it is forbidden as the primary practice to cook the meat of an impure animal with pure milk (or vice versa), due to appearance — since an onlooker would think this is pure meat with pure milk, and would also suspect the cook of wanting to eat something forbidden. But for medicinal purposes, even for a patient with no life-threatening illness, it is permitted to cook this way.
takeaways: The Torah-level prohibition of meat and milk also applies to the meat of a nevelah/treifah pure animal, but not to the meat of an impure animal with pure milk (or vice versa) — there it is Torah-permitted but forbidden as the primary practice due to appearance; permitted for medicine.

paragraphs: Besar chayya veop, apillu bachaleb behema tehora muttar bebishshul ubahanaa, mishshum deeno asur min hattora baakila ella besar behema tehora bachaleb behema tehora, abal besar chayya veop, issuro baakila hu midderabbanan, lekak muttar bebishshul ubahanaa. veyesh machmirim leasero midderabbanan gam bebishshul ubahanaa; veayyen "erek-hashshulchan", ot d' veot y"d, yeuyyan sham. uleinyan halaka: hammachmir bebishshul, tabo alayv beraka, abal bahanaa achar shennitbashshel, en rauy lehachmir leabbed mamon yisrael, ella im nizdammen shennitbashshel besar op o chayya bechalab, yimkerennu legoy; ubebishshul yesh taam lehachmir mishshum marit haayin.

clarification.explanation: The meat of a wild animal (such as a deer) or fowl, even with the milk of a pure domestic animal, is Torah-permitted for cooking and benefit, since the Torah's prohibition applies only to the meat of a pure domestic animal with the milk of a pure domestic animal, whereas the prohibition of wild animal or fowl meat with milk is only rabbinic — and is therefore permitted for cooking and benefit. Some are stringent and forbid this rabbinically, both for cooking and benefit. The practical halacha: one who is stringent regarding cooking is praiseworthy, but if fowl or wild animal meat was already cooked in milk, it is not proper to be stringent and lose the money (by discarding rather than selling to a gentile) — rather it is recommended to sell it to a gentile. Regarding the cooking itself, there is reason to be stringent, due to appearance.
takeaways: Wild animal and fowl meat with milk is Torah-permitted for cooking and benefit (only rabbinically forbidden); one who is stringent about cooking is praiseworthy, but if already cooked, it is better to sell it to a gentile than to discard it.

paragraphs: Besar behema tehora bachaleb chayya tehora, eno asur min hattora, ella asur midderabbanan; veeno asur ella baakila, abal bahanaa muttar; veasur lebashshel lekattechilla, mippene marit haayin.

clarification.explanation: The meat of a pure domestic animal with the milk of a pure wild animal (such as a deer) is not Torah-forbidden at all, only rabbinically, and even this only for eating — but it is permitted for benefit. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to cook it as the primary practice, due to appearance.
takeaways: Domestic animal meat with wild animal milk (not domestic milk) is only rabbinically forbidden for eating, permitted for benefit, but forbidden to cook as the primary practice due to appearance.

paragraphs: Im kabash chalab biqdera meet leet, dehaynu k"d shaot shelemot, veaach"k bishshel baqqedera hahi besar behema - hattabshil asur bahanaa; d"g shehaqqedera lo balea hechalab ella "y kebisha, mikkol maqom aach"k paleta oto hechalab shebbah letok habbasar "y bishshul, veasur min hattora; abal im lo bishshelu beotah qedera besar behema, ella besar chayya veop, en hattabshil asur bahanaa ella raq baakila. veayyen mishbetzot zahab, sop seip qatan , umachaziq beraka, ot b'.

clarification.explanation: If milk was soaked in a pot for a full day (24 hours — "pickling"), and afterward domestic animal meat was cooked in that same pot — the dish is forbidden for benefit, since even though the pot did not absorb the milk immediately but only through pickling, it nevertheless released the absorbed milk into the meat during cooking — and this is already Torah-forbidden. But if wild animal or fowl meat, rather than domestic animal meat, was cooked in that pot, the dish is forbidden only for eating, not for benefit.
takeaways: A pot that absorbed milk through a day's pickling, then used to cook domestic animal meat — the dish is Torah-forbidden for benefit; with wild animal/fowl meat — forbidden only for eating.

paragraphs: Hambashshel bachaleb gediyya shello hayniqa, sheyyesh lah chalab keshehi qeroba lime ledatah, chayyab min hattora, vekannizkar baggemara dechullin, dap qy"g, ammud b. veayyen "maaseh-roqeach", cheleq b, bepereq t mehilkot maakalot asurot, halaka v', ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: One who cooks meat in the milk of a young goat that has not yet nursed kids but has milk because she is close to giving birth is Torah-liable for this, as explained in the Gemara in tractate Chullin.
takeaways: Even the milk of a goat that has not yet given birth (but has milk in anticipation of birth) is considered "milk" for the Torah-level prohibition of meat and milk.

paragraphs: Tzir hayyotze "y melicha, venapal letok hattabshil shel chalab venitbashshel, asur bahanaa min hattora. veayyen machaziq beraka, ot y"d.

clarification.explanation: Brine (the liquid that emerges from meat as a result of salting) that fell into a dairy dish and was cooked within it is Torah-forbidden for benefit, since the brine itself is considered meat for this purpose.
takeaways: Brine that emerged from meat during salting, falling into a dairy dish and cooked, has the law of actual meat, forbidding the dish for benefit by Torah law.

paragraphs: Qedera shel chalab sheenah bat-yoma shebbishshel bah basar, eno ober mishshum bishshul; velo od, ella shemmuttar lekattechilla lebashshel bah basar legoy, o leezeh tzorek sheen bo akila; veen leesor mishshum marit haayin, demi yodea im hi qedera shel basar o shel chalab, ukemo shekkatab "pitche-teshuba", seip qatan ch, beshem "chamude-daniyyel". mihu, im hi qedera gedola yoter midday, sheen derek lebashshel bah chalab, ella raq tabshil shel basar bisudot gedolot, "p shehi enah bat-yoma, asur lebashshel bah chalab, kegon sheyyesh lo chema harbeh sherotzeh lehittika biqdera gedola letzorek haggoy, ki zo haqqedera, chazutah meid aleha shehi shel basar, veyesh lachush lemarit haayin, sheen yodeim shehu mebashshel letzorek haggoy.

clarification.explanation: A dairy pot that is not "within its day" (more than 24 hours have passed since it was used for milk, so its absorbed taste has already spoiled), in which meat was then cooked — carries no cooking prohibition. Furthermore, it is even permitted as the primary practice to cook meat in it for a gentile, or for any non-eating purpose — with no concern for appearance, since no one can tell whether it is a meat or dairy pot. But if it is an especially large pot, not normally used to cook milk (only meat dishes for large feasts) — then even if not within its day, it is forbidden to cook milk in it, for example if one wishes to melt a large quantity of butter in it for a gentile — since the large pot's appearance identifies it as a meat pot, and there is concern for appearance, since no one would see that it is being cooked for a gentile's sake.
takeaways: A dairy pot not within its day may be used to cook meat, even as the primary practice for a gentile, with no concern for appearance.
But an especially large pot (normally only for meat feasts) may not be used for milk even when not within its day, since its size identifies it as a meat pot.

paragraphs: Basar bechalab sheasur bahanaa, veaach"k nitareb mimmennu betabshil shel yeraqot o orez vekaddomeh, veen battabshil hahu shishshim lebattel habbasar bechalab hannizkar - muttar limkor lenakeri chutz middeme issur shebbo; dekol issure hanaa, apillu yesh bahem benoten taam, muttar limkor lenakeri chutz middeme issur shebbo; veayyen "peri-megadim" bipticha, umishbetzot zahab, seip qatan b'.

clarification.explanation: Meat and milk forbidden for benefit, which afterward became mixed into a vegetable or rice dish and the like, without sixty times its volume in the dish to nullify the meat-and-milk mixture within it — may nevertheless be sold to a gentile, provided the value of the forbidden portion is deducted from the sale price. This follows from the general rule: all benefit-forbidden substances, even those that "impart taste" (that is, the taste is noticeable in the dish), may be sold to a gentile as long as the value of the forbidden portion is deducted.
takeaways: A permitted dish mixed with meat-and-milk (without sixty times its volume for nullification) may be sold to a gentile, deducting the value of the forbidden portion.

paragraphs: Basar tzali bechalab, asur min hattora, vaapillu bahanaa, detzali biklal bishshul hu vekannizkar baacharonim. veken hamtaggen basar bechalab, asur min hattora, veasur bahanaa. velaken nerot shel cheleb shearebu hannakerim bahem chema veqanu yisrael mehem, asur lehadliqan utzerikin qebura; ayyen machaziq beraka, ot t"v. ak nerot sheyyesh bahem sapeq im erebu chema vechalab yachad, yesh lehattir mikkoach sepeq sepeqa; rotzeh lomar: sapeq im yesh chema, veim timtze lemor yesh, shemma nitbattela beshishshim; veod yesh sapeq shelishi: ulay halaka keman deamar en issur bahanaa ella midderabbanan. umihu lekattechilla lo yiqneh minnerot ellu; veayyen "yosep ometz" siman p"g.

clarification.explanation: Meat roasted in milk is Torah-forbidden, including for benefit, since roasting is considered "cooking" for this purpose. Likewise fried meat in milk — Torah-forbidden and forbidden for benefit. Therefore candles made of milk (hardened animal fat/milk substance) into which gentiles mixed butter, which a Jew bought — may not be lit, and require "burial" (disposal, as in halacha 3). But if there is doubt whether butter was mixed with milk in these candles, one may be lenient by force of a "double doubt" (compounding two doubts): doubt whether there is any butter in the candle at all, and if there is, doubt whether it was nullified in sixty, plus a third doubt — perhaps according to a certain opinion the benefit-prohibition here is only rabbinic. But despite this, it is preferable as the primary practice not to buy such candles.
takeaways: Meat roasted or fried in milk is Torah-forbidden even for benefit, like cooking; milk candles mixed with butter may not be lit and require burial, unless there is a double doubt allowing after-the-fact leniency — but it is preferable not to buy such candles.

paragraphs: Im bishshelu chema biqdera shel basar bat-yoma, veneesra dela haya shishshim, asur lehadliq bechema zo, daasura bahanaa. vegam nerot chanukka, deen mishtammeshin leorah, asur lehadliq bechema zo. veayyen machaziq beraka. veim hiddichu kele basar bemayim rotechin, veken hiddichu kele chalab bikli acher bemayim rotechin, venitarebu zeh bazeh beodam rotechin, asurin bahanaa utzerikin qebura. bammeh debarim amurim? berotechin dikli rishon shehayyad soledet bo, dehave bishshul, abal keli sheni, "g demaplit umablia, eno mebashshel, umuttarim hammayim bahanaa. veayyen "kereti upeleti" vesipte daat ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: If butter was cooked in a meat pot that was within its day (used for meat that same day) and became forbidden because there was no sixty to nullify the meat taste — it is forbidden to light with this butter, since it is forbidden for benefit, and this includes Chanukah candles, whose light one may not use even for the sake of a mitzvah. Likewise, if a meat vessel was rinsed with boiling water, and separately a dairy vessel was rinsed with boiling water in a different vessel, and the water from both rinsings mixed together while still boiling — the water is forbidden for benefit and requires burial. This is true specifically when it concerns boiling water in a "first vessel" (a vessel on the fire, hot enough to burn a hand), which is considered cooking; but if it is a "second vessel" (water transferred to another vessel, not on the fire), even though it does release and dissolve tastes, it is not considered cooking, and therefore the water is permitted for benefit.
takeaways: Butter forbidden by cooking in a meat pot is forbidden for benefit, including use in candles (even Chanukah candles).
Hot rinse water from meat and dairy vessels mixing while boiling is forbidden for benefit and requires burial, only if in a first vessel (on the fire); in a second vessel, it is permitted.

paragraphs: Dagim bechalab muttar apillu midderabbanan, mihu yesh bahem sakkanat choli ulekak asur leakelam. vehu haddin leekol dagim im gebina yesh sakkanat choli, abal dagim bechema - yesh min haacharonim shekkatebu deen chashash choli bazeh, veyesh shekkatebu deikka chashash choli. veshomer napsho yirchaq veyizzaher, deha apillu harab "pachad-yitzchaq" shehaya rope gadol, venireh lo deen bazeh nezeq, nimna milleekol. upoh irenu bagdad en metaggenim dagim bechema, dechosheshin hachashash hannizkar.

clarification.explanation: Fish with milk is permitted even rabbinically, but there is concern of health danger involved, and for this reason it is forbidden to eat (a concern of danger is considered a full halachic prohibition, not merely a recommendation). Eating fish with cheese likewise involves a similar health concern. Regarding fish with butter — some of the later authorities wrote there is no concern of harm at all, and some wrote there is concern. The Ben Ish Chai recommends being careful, since even Rabbi "Pachad Yitzchak," who was a great physician and held there was no harm in it, nevertheless personally avoided eating it. The Baghdad custom is to avoid frying fish in butter, due to this same concern.
takeaways: Fish with milk is permitted under the meat-and-milk law, but forbidden for eating due to health-danger concern (a full halachic prohibition); regarding butter there is medical dispute, and the Baghdad custom is to avoid it as a stringency.

paragraphs: Betzim shennimtzaim tok hattarnegolet: im hem gemurot bechelbon vechelmon, muttar min haddin leakelam bechalab, abal im en lah ella raq chelmon bilbad, asur leakelam bechalab. veim akela bipne atzmah, muttar leekol achareha chalab; veyesh machmirin bazeh. v"g deamerinan: im hem gemurot muttar leakelam bechalab, haynu mishshurat-haddin, abal nahagu shello leakelam bechalab; veken hamminhag poh irenu; vegam molechim otah lebaddah, o al gab basar; umikkol maqom, im napela letabshil, enah oseret.

clarification.explanation: Eggs found inside a chicken (not yet laid): if they are already complete with full white and yolk — by strict law it is permitted to eat them with milk. But if they contain only yolk alone (not yet developed), it is forbidden to eat them with milk. And if one ate this egg alone (without meat), it is permitted to eat milk right afterward, though some are stringent about this. Nevertheless, although by strict law complete eggs are permitted with milk, the custom is not to eat them with milk anyway — and so is the Baghdad custom, where they are also salted alone or together with meat. But if such an egg fell by mistake into a dish, it does not forbid it.
takeaways: A complete egg found inside a chicken is by strict law permitted with milk, but the custom is to be stringent and not eat it that way; an egg that fell by mistake into a dish does not forbid it.

paragraphs: Chalab hannimtza beqeba, yizzaher lekattechilla shello lehannicho beqeba ad sheyyitztannen hechalab tok haqqeba, mippene shecheleb haqqeba hu charip vechimmutz; ubediabad en lachush veshari lehaamid bo. upoh irenu nohagin lehotzi tekep umiyyad et hechalab min haqqeba qodem sheyyitztannen; veim shaha hechalab betok haqqeba k"d shaot, have lah kabush, veasur lehaamid bo lekattechilla - ben betzalul, ben beqarush; ubediabad shekkebar heemid bo, muttar apillu heemid betzalul; ken hu daat mera"n za"l deqayma lan kevateh, ak mvr"m za"l oser betzalul gam bediabad. veim haya sapeq tzalul o qarush, az gam lehaashkenazzim deazeli batar pisqe mvr"m, azelinan lequlla umuttar. veayyen karet upeleti za"l.

clarification.explanation: The milk (rennet) found in an animal's stomach (used for curdling cheese) — it is good to be careful as the primary practice not to leave it inside the stomach until it cools, since the stomach's rennet is sharp and sour and can quickly absorb meat taste. After the fact, if it was left this way, there is no concern, and it is kosher for setting cheese. The Baghdad custom is to remove the rennet from the stomach immediately, before it cools. If the rennet was left in the stomach for a full 24 hours, this is considered like "pickling," and it is forbidden as the primary practice to set cheese with it — whether the rennet is still liquid or has already curdled. But after the fact, if cheese was already set this way, it is permitted, even if the rennet was liquid at the time of setting — this is Maran's view, which is followed, although the Rema forbids liquid rennet even after the fact. In a case of doubt whether the rennet was liquid or curdled, even the Ashkenazim (who follow the Rema) are lenient.
takeaways: Rennet left in the stomach 24 hours is considered pickled and forbidden as the primary practice for setting cheese; after the fact, permitted even if liquid (following Maran), and in a case of doubt, even Ashkenazim are lenient.

paragraphs: Yesh mattirin lehannicha keli sheyyesh bo chalab etzel keli sheyyesh bo basar tok teba achat, vela chayeshinan shemma yippol mizzeh lazeh velo yeda. veyesh machmirin lekattechilla, umatzrikin sheyyihyu shenehem mekussim; veken rauy lehizzaher bekak. veen mannichim keli sheyyesh bo chalab etzel keli sheyyesh bo melach, ella im ken meruchaqim zeh mizzeh vegam mekussim, deyesh lachush lisbarat rashi"y velisbarat haramba"m za"l. mihu kol zeh lekattechilla, abal im abar vehinnicha, muttar bediabad likli alema; veim eno mannicha beqeba, ella beaqray addata litlo miyyad - happeri chadash oser vehapperi toar mattir.

clarification.explanation: Some permit placing a dairy vessel and a meat vessel together in the same cabinet, with no concern that something might spill from one to the other unnoticed. Some are stringent, requiring as the primary practice that both vessels be covered, and it is proper to be careful this way. A dairy vessel should not be placed next to a salt vessel (unless they are distanced from each other and covered), for halachic reasons connected to the views of Rashi and the Rambam. All this is stated as the primary practice, but if they were nevertheless placed together, it is permitted after the fact for all the vessels. And if the placement is only temporary, with the intent to remove the vessel immediately (not a permanent placement) — there is a dispute: the "Peri Chadash" forbids and the "Peri To'ar" permits.
takeaways: As the primary practice, one should be careful to cover (or separate) dairy and meat vessels in the same cabinet, and likewise dairy and salt; after the fact, it is permitted.

paragraphs: Sigrah shemmadliqah minner shel cheleb, lo yadliq min happetila, ella yadliq min hashshalhebet; vehammachmir gam bazeh, tabo alayv beraka. vekol zeh beshoep bepiv beet hahadlaqa, abal im madliqah beyado beli sheipa, veachar shemmesira min hanner shoep bepiv, muttar lekulle alema.

clarification.explanation: One who lights a cigarette from a milk candle should not light it from the wick itself (since then he inhales smoke that passed through the dairy wick's flame while inhaling), but should light it from the flame itself, and one who is stringent about this too is praiseworthy. All this applies specifically when he inhales with his mouth at the moment of lighting itself; but if he lights the cigarette by hand without inhaling, and only inhales after removing it from the candle — this is permitted according to all opinions.
takeaways: One lighting a cigarette from a milk candle should draw from the flame, not the wick itself; if lit by hand without inhaling during lighting, it is permitted according to all opinions.
